title: Hank's Wedding

jokes.text: Adam Sandler performs 'My Little Chicken' — a love song to a chicken that includes 'I love the way you eat gravel to help you digest' and 'If an egg can fit in there, why can't I?'
jokes.setup: The song begins as a sincere, tender love ballad — 'When I'm feeling down and feeling sad, you come around and make me glad'
jokes.punchline: The object of affection is revealed to be a literal chicken, with increasingly absurd anatomical details culminating in 'if an egg can fit in there, why can't I?'
jokes.explanation: A genuine piece of absurdist comedy that escalates beautifully. The gravel-eating line is a perfect non-sequitur that signals the audience we've left normal territory, and the final egg line is a genuinely filthy, well-earned payoff that catches you off guard. Sandler's mode is character-specific but the writers built a tight comedic song structure around a truly weird premise. High impact because it's live, energetic, and the audience applauds. Scores slightly lower on character integration since it's a guest performance, not character-driven Sanders Show comedy.

dialogue.line: ♪ My little chicken ♪

jokes.text: Hank proposes marriage on live television to a woman nobody on the show knew he was dating. Larry's stunned 'What?' captures his complete blindsiding.
jokes.setup: Hank asks Larry if he can 'talk to someone' at the end of the show — innocuous enough — and then delivers a marriage proposal to Margaret on live TV
jokes.punchline: Larry's genuine 'What?' captures total bewilderment; followed by his line 'I have GOT to start coming to rehearsal'
jokes.explanation: A standout structural joke: the payoff works on two levels simultaneously. The absurdity of Hank proposing on air to a woman nobody knew about is the primary joke, but Larry's 'What?' is the perfect single-word punchline — pure reaction comedy, deeply in character for the show's observational style. Then 'I have GOT to start coming to rehearsal' is a second, beautifully economical punchline that reframes the shock as professional failure rather than personal surprise — which is classically Larry. High character integration because only Larry Sanders, the host of a show spinning out of his control, could deliver this line.

dialogue.speaker: Adam Sandler
dialogue.line: ♪ I love your breasts ♪

jokes.text: 'I have got to start coming to rehearsal.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just proposed on live TV without telling anyone
jokes.punchline: Larry's response frames the emotional chaos of a surprise proposal entirely as a professional/logistical failure — he's annoyed he wasn't in the loop, not touched
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and a thesis statement for Larry's character. Maximum economy — six words, no waste. The joke reframes an emotionally significant moment (a marriage proposal) entirely through the lens of professional control anxiety. It could ONLY be Larry Sanders: a man so consumed by his show's operation that his first instinct after a surprise proposal is to note his own production negligence. This is the kind of line that gets quoted. Scores very high on character integration and economy — it's perfectly calibrated understatement.

dialogue.line: ♪ I love the way You eat gravel / To help you digest ♪

jokes.text: 'What the fuck do you think that is, huh? What is this, love connection?'
jokes.setup: Hank has just proposed on live TV — a romantic, crowd-pleasing moment
jokes.punchline: Artie, furious, immediately pivots to 'Love Connection' — a dating show reference that both deflates the romance and reveals his complete exasperation at being ambushed on air
jokes.explanation: Artie's anger cutting through the sweetness of a proposal is deeply on-brand for the show's backstage cynicism. 'Love Connection' is a sharp, period-specific pop culture jab that locates the absurdity of doing this on television. The rapid-fire delivery ('huh? huh?') adds to the comic energy. Slightly less original than some of Artie's best work but executes the character's voice cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Adam Sandler
dialogue.line: ♪ But I know / That the worst I should fear / Is a slight case Of salmonella ♪

jokes.text: 'All right, go ahead, Artie. Go ahead. Come on. Take your best shot. You can't hurt me. I'm invincible. I got the shield of love around me.'
jokes.setup: Artie is clearly livid at Hank for the surprise proposal; Hank is in a euphoric post-proposal glow
jokes.punchline: 'I got the shield of love around me' — Hank's grandiose, sincere self-description in the face of Artie's fury is both absurd and deeply in character
jokes.explanation: Tambor's delivery sells this completely. 'Shield of love' is a genuinely funny phrase for its grandiosity — it's Hank inflating a romantic moment into mythological protection. The comedy comes from the gap between Hank's blissful self-image and the very real professional and personal chaos he's caused. Character-specific and quotable.

dialogue.line: ♪ If an egg can fit in there, Why can't i? ♪

jokes.text: 'Oh, yeah? You mean you were serious?' / 'Yes, I'm quite serious.' / 'You're serious.'
jokes.setup: Hank just proposed on live TV; Artie cannot process that this was real
jokes.punchline: Artie's repeated, stunned 'You're serious?' — delivered as if he genuinely hoped this was an elaborate prank — is the comedic beat of disbelief landing
jokes.explanation: A good comedic beat of incredulity. Artie's 'you're serious' echoing back is classic straight-man disbelief and works well in context, though it's not a particularly original construction. Functional, honest to character, effective in the scene.

jokes.text: 'She happens to be Regional Sales Manager for the Sandwich King.'
jokes.setup: Artie scoffs 'An actress' — the obvious showbiz concern about a gold-digger
jokes.punchline: Margaret's mundane real-world job — 'Regional Sales Manager for the Sandwich King' — is the anti-showbiz punchline; the specificity of 'Sandwich King' makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: 'Sandwich King' is doing real comedic work here — it's specific enough to be absurd but plausible enough to be grounded. The joke subverts the expected 'actress/gold-digger' concern by replacing it with something so ordinary it circles back to being funny. Good economy and structure: setup is one word ('actress'), payoff is one perfectly weird proper noun.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have got to start Coming to rehearsal.

jokes.text: 'I sort of kept her under wraps. I figured you guys would make fun of me.' / 'We wouldn't do that.' / 'Not to your face.'
jokes.setup: Hank explains he hid the relationship because he feared ridicule; Larry assures him they wouldn't mock him
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately undercuts Larry's reassurance with 'Not to your face' — honest and devastating
jokes.explanation: Four words ('Not to your face') that perfectly crystallize the show's ethos: showbiz politeness barely concealing constant judgment. It's honest, mean, and funny in a way that exposes the Larry/Artie relationship as simultaneously caring and merciless. High economy and character integration — this is exactly how Artie operates, and it lands like a perfectly timed knife. Quotable and reusable as a general-purpose line.

jokes.text: 'Should I get a bundt cake?'
jokes.setup: Hank excitedly announces Margaret is coming to the studio and wants everyone to greet her warmly
jokes.punchline: Larry's instinct is a bizarrely specific, slightly passive-aggressive domestic gesture — 'a bundt cake'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'bundt cake' is the joke — Larry's idea of warmth is a stiff, slightly formal baked good. It's a small character comedy beat that reveals his social awkwardness beneath the professional polish. The word 'bundt' is inherently funny. Clean, economical, works.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You can't hurt me. I'm invincible. I got the shield Of love around me.

jokes.text: 'Please, no pictures.'
jokes.setup: Margaret says 'It's an honor to meet you' — a sincere, slightly starstruck greeting
jokes.punchline: Larry's reflexive 'Please, no pictures' — as if she's a paparazzo, not his co-worker's fiancée — exposes his paranoid celebrity ego
jokes.explanation: Three-word joke that says everything about Larry's character: he cannot receive sincere admiration without reflexively activating celebrity-management mode. It's absurd in context, instantly recognizable as a character tic, and perfectly economical. Could only be Larry Sanders. One of the episode's more quietly sharp character comedy moments.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Wall of love, my ass.

jokes.text: The temp agency confusion: Margaret greets Beverly, who confirms 'Yes, margaret, hi. Um... I'm margaret. / I'm Sharon. I'm from the temp agency.'
jokes.setup: Hank is introducing his fiancée to the staff; someone called 'Beverly' is greeted
jokes.punchline: The person greeted isn't Beverly at all — she's Sharon from the temp agency, revealing the chaos and anonymity of the show's workplace
jokes.explanation: A competent workplace comedy beat about the interchangeability of support staff and the chaos of a live television show. The confusion lands mildly but isn't especially crafted — it's more of a grounded observational moment than a sharp joke. Gets a chuckle in the room.

jokes.text: 'The woman's clearly half his age. They've known each other two weeks. And Artie, she worked for some guy named, what, the Sandwich King?' / 'I believe that's a product.'
jokes.setup: Larry is rattling off his concerns about Margaret — culminating in the Sandwich King reference as if it's a sketchy employer
jokes.punchline: Artie's dry correction — 'I believe that's a product' — punctures Larry's conspiratorial tone by clarifying the mundane reality
jokes.explanation: A callback that earns its callback status — 'Sandwich King' is funny the first time as a specific detail, and Artie's deadpan correction ('I believe that's a product') is a new angle on the same joke that also characterizes his role as reality-check. Good economy and character integration for Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We wouldn't Do that. Not to your face.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie's competing marriage records: 'I'm on my fourth wife and, uh—' / 'Fifth.' / 'You— well, whatever. And you, of course—' / 'No, no, no, don't.'
jokes.setup: Larry is questioning who they are to give marital advice to Hank
jokes.punchline: Artie corrects Larry on his own wife count (Larry lost track), and then cuts off any reciprocal analysis — implying his own situation is worse or equally disqualifying
jokes.explanation: The joke that Larry doesn't know how many wives Artie has had — and Artie immediately shutting down any reciprocal examination — is rich character comedy. It establishes both men as spectacular failures at the institution they're critiquing, which gives the whole scene an ironic foundation. The quick rhythm of the exchange is well-calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Should I get A bundt cake?

jokes.text: Larry: 'And you, of course—' (implying Artie's marriage failures) / Artie: 'No, no, no, don't.'
jokes.setup: Larry is building a case that neither of them is qualified to criticize Hank's marriage by listing their own failures.
jokes.punchline: Artie cuts him off before he can even finish — 'No, no, no, don't' — suggesting Artie's marital history is SO bad he won't even let it be named.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the incomplete sentence — whatever Artie's marital history is, it's bad enough that he won't allow it to be spoken aloud. Classic negative-space comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Please, no pictures.

jokes.text: 'What is Hank doing with someone so normal?' (delivered as if 'normal' is the alarming quality)
jokes.setup: The men are trying to articulate what's off about Margaret; they reach for obvious criticisms (too young, too pretty) and then Larry lands on the real concern
jokes.punchline: 'Normal' is the genuinely suspicious quality in this showbiz world — it's the word that reveals the characters' total immersion in industry unreality
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent observational joke about the entertainment industry's warped values. 'Normal' being treated as the suspicious trait perfectly captures the show's Hollywood satire angle. It's earned — it comes from a real place of character logic — and it's the most insightful line in the scene. Good originality for a single word doing so much work.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You must be Beverly.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: Yes, margaret, hi.

dialogue.speaker: Sharon

jokes.text: 'You're a very talented... Successful show-biz personality. Any woman would want to marry that.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to reassure Hank that he's a catch
jokes.punchline: The hesitation before 'successful show-biz personality' and the construction 'any woman would want to marry that' — referring to Hank as a commodity ('that') rather than a person — is subtly devastating
jokes.explanation: The cruelty is in the framing — Larry can't bring himself to call Hank 'talented' outright, hedges with 'successful show-biz personality,' and then refers to Hank's identity as 'that' — as if he's a brand package, not a man. It's characteristic of the show's layered insincerity and lands as dark comedy beneath a surface of reassurance.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The woman's clearly Half his age. They've known Each other two weeks.

jokes.text: 'No offense, Artie.' (after asking Larry to be best man)
jokes.setup: Hank has just given Larry an emotional speech about love and asked him to be best man
jokes.punchline: The perfunctory 'No offense, Artie' — delivered as a completely inadequate afterthought to a deeply offensive exclusion of the man who has devoted his career to this show
jokes.explanation: The brevity is the joke — 'no offense, Artie' is laughably insufficient given the context. Artie's non-response (he just says 'I would be happy to, Hank' — to Hank's line to Larry) adds to the awkwardness. Classic cringe-adjacent character comedy that is distinctly Larry Sanders Show in its understated brutality.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I believe that's a product.

jokes.text: 'I hope Margaret and I can be as happy as you and Francine.' / 'That is the most cynical pile of bullshit that I have ever heard in my entire life.'
jokes.setup: Hank sincerely invokes Larry's marriage as a model of happiness — a genuinely warm sentiment
jokes.punchline: Artie's explosion — 'the most cynical pile of bullshit I have ever heard in my entire life' — implies Larry's marriage is such an obvious disaster that this comment reads as mockery
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Hank is sincere, which makes it funnier; Artie's massive overreaction implies the Larry/Francine marriage is more of a disaster than we've been told; and 'most cynical pile of bullshit I have ever heard in my entire life' is a great Artie line — hyperbolic, authoritative, final. Character integration is high because this reaction is pure Artie, and the structural setup/subversion is clean.

dialogue.line: I'm on my fourth wife And, uh-- Fifth.

jokes.text: 'Do you want broccoli? No. No?'
jokes.setup: Immediately after Artie's explosive 'cynical bullshit' declaration, there's an abrupt, banal cut to someone offering broccoli
jokes.punchline: The complete non-sequitur deflation — someone is just offering broccoli in the middle of this emotional showdown
jokes.explanation: A small deflation beat — the everyday intrusion of food into a dramatic moment. Works as a tonal punctuation mark but is not especially crafted; the humor is situational and mild.

jokes.text: Larry: 'She obviously wants something from him.' Artie: 'Not every single woman in the whole world wants something from you. We're not talking about me.'
jokes.setup: Larry projects suspicion onto Margaret; Artie calls it out
jokes.punchline: Larry's correction 'We're not talking about me' is too quick and too specific — confirming that he did, in fact, immediately make it about himself
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Larry's unconscious self-referentiality — he cannot discuss anyone else's life without it becoming about his own fears. 'We're not talking about me' is the tell. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: She's too pretty. She's too young. What is Hank doing With someone so normal?

jokes.text: 'Your mother said what?' / 'My lawyer.' / 'Your— oh.'
jokes.setup: Francine says 'My lawyer said to clean you out, and I said no'
jokes.punchline: Larry mishears 'lawyer' as 'mother' — revealing his deep suspicion of Francine's family — then catches himself
jokes.explanation: A quick misunderstanding joke that does double duty — the gag itself is funny, but the 'your mother?' slip also characterizes Larry as paranoid and suspicious of Francine's support network. Short, clean, structurally tight. The 'your— oh' is a perfectly naturalistic stammer of correction.

dialogue.line: Me?

jokes.text: 'Stop yelling at me!' / 'God, if Hank could only see us like this.' [whispers] 'If Hank could only see us like this.' / 'What?' / 'Nothing.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine are mid-fight about their marriage while Larry was ostensibly warning Hank about rushing into marriage
jokes.punchline: Larry catches himself mid-ironic observation — whispers it again as if savoring it — then denies having said anything when Francine asks
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed moment of self-awareness: Larry sees the irony of their situation, can't help saying it, then re-whispers it to himself because he finds it so satisfying — then immediately retreats into denial. This is very specifically Larry Sanders behavior: self-aware enough to notice the irony, cowardly enough to not own it. The second whisper is the key beat — it's the behavior of a man who amuses himself. High character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. Me neither.

jokes.text: 'What does this fish look like to you?' / 'Um... Danny DeVito?' / 'Nicholson.' / 'Oh, yeah. I can see that.'
jokes.setup: Larry enters and is immediately shown a fish-shaped desk piece that looks like a celebrity
jokes.punchline: The mismatch of answers (DeVito vs. Nicholson) and the earnest debate about a fish prop's celebrity resemblance is the joke
jokes.explanation: A light absurdist beat that works as a tonal reset after the domestic tension. The specificity of DeVito vs. Nicholson makes it funnier than a generic answer. Functional comedy that earns a chuckle without demanding too much.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Larry, we rarely Discuss our feelings, But I love you As much as that girl.

jokes.text: 'I bet you want to have the wedding on the show.' / 'My god. How could you possibly know that?' / 'You should know by now I can see into your soul.'
jokes.setup: Hank comes in excited; Larry immediately predicts exactly what Hank wants without Hank saying a word
jokes.punchline: Hank's genuine shock at Larry's prediction; Larry's deadpan 'I can see into your soul' — which is funny because Hank is so transparent that a blind man could predict this
jokes.explanation: Larry's ability to predict Hank's every move — and Hank's genuine awe at being 'read' — is a wonderful character comedy beat. The joke is that Hank is so nakedly predictable that Larry's 'soul-reading' is actually just paying minimal attention. 'That's really spooky' from the onlooker is a nice button. Good character integration for both men.

jokes.text: 'The Liebowitz bar mitzvah is booked that week.'
jokes.setup: Hank is pitching the wedding show as his 'dream come true'; Artie is trying to pump the brakes
jokes.punchline: Artie invokes the 'Liebowitz bar mitzvah' as a scheduling conflict — a specific, mundane, slightly absurd competing event that deflates Hank's romanticism
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Liebowitz bar mitzvah' is the joke — it's exactly the kind of mundane production booking that would clash with a sweeping romantic gesture on a TV show. Artie wielding it as a bureaucratic weapon against Hank's dream is pure character comedy.

jokes.text: 'May I remind you of my old friend Tiny Tim?' / 'As I recall, that was a freak show.' / 'A highly rated one.'
jokes.setup: Larry resists the wedding-on-TV concept; Artie advocates for it using the classic Tonight Show Tiny Tim wedding precedent
jokes.punchline: Larry calls it a 'freak show'; Artie's 'A highly rated one' concedes the point entirely while doubling down — ratings justify everything
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The Tiny Tim reference is a real, specific piece of late-night television history (the 1969 Tonight Show wedding), and using it here is an insider joke that rewards knowledgeable viewers. But the real craft is in Artie's response: 'A highly rated one' is a perfect four-word summation of the show's central theme — the entertainment industry's willingness to exploit anything for ratings. It's delivered as a complete moral concession with zero shame, which is exactly who Artie is. High character integration, economy, and earned quality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: [Whispers] If Hank could only See us like this.

jokes.text: 'You want high ratings? Let's do 'Who Shot Hank Kingsley?''
jokes.setup: The group is debating whether to do the wedding show for ratings
jokes.punchline: Larry's suggestion — murdering Hank as a TV concept — is a meta reference to 'Who Shot JR?' and a dark joke about how expendable Hank is in Larry's eyes
jokes.explanation: A sharp dark comedy moment — Larry floating a murder-mystery premise as a legitimate ratings alternative to a wedding show. The meta-referential layer (the Dallas 'Who Shot JR?' format) adds a comedic dimension for TV-literate viewers, and the fact that Larry suggests it completely casually makes it funnier. 'Please, Larry, not even as a joke' from Hank is a perfect straight-man button.

jokes.text: 'I want it to be a tasteful testament to marriage.' / [Artie] 'Hank, three words — Luke and Laura.' / 'Say no more. We understand each other.'
jokes.setup: Hank insists the wedding shouldn't be 'a circus' but a 'tasteful testament to marriage'
jokes.punchline: Artie invokes Luke and Laura — the General Hospital super-couple whose 1981 wedding drew 30 million viewers — as shorthand for 'big, exploitative television event'; Hank immediately abandons all his 'tasteful' principles
jokes.explanation: Another insider TV reference that rewards knowledge — Luke and Laura is perfect shorthand for 'massive, circus-level television event.' The speed at which Hank capitulates ('Say no more. We understand each other') after his principled speech about tastefulness is the real joke: Hank's principles last exactly as long as it takes to mention a high-rated precedent. Character integration is high.

jokes.text: 'Are you going to wear tails?' / [Artie, already dialing] 'Yes, I am. I'm going to make a call.'
jokes.setup: They've just agreed to do the wedding show; Hank excitedly asks if Artie will wear tails
jokes.punchline: Artie confirms he's wearing tails and is already on the phone — he's been plotting the production while ostensibly having an emotional conversation
jokes.explanation: A competent character beat — Artie seamlessly transitions from the personal to the professional without any visible gear-shift because for him there's no difference. The tails detail is a nice absurd touch. Functional comedy that reinforces character without achieving anything special.

jokes.text: Artie: 'That was personal. This is business.' (After Francine accused him of not staying out of it.)
jokes.setup: Artie said he would stay out of the wedding drama, then immediately dove in.
jokes.punchline: The Godfather-style distinction between 'personal' and 'business' applied to a late-night TV wedding is Artie's brand of grandiosity.
jokes.explanation: A competent Artie beat. The Corleone logic is a familiar character trait but well-deployed here. Doesn't rise to exceptional but is completely in his voice.

jokes.text: 'After this so-called wedding show, that man will be married to that woman.' / 'Yes.' / 'Now, that is what I call great television.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to articulate why the wedding show is a bad idea
jokes.punchline: Artie's pivot — acknowledging the potential disaster of the marriage as what makes it 'great television' — is a cynical, perfect summation of the entertainment industry's relationship to human suffering
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and a genuine thesis statement for the series. Artie's 'Now, that is what I call great television' is funny because it's simultaneously a prediction of marital failure AND an endorsement of that failure as entertainment value. The line is delivered with Artie's characteristic gravitas, which makes the nihilism funnier. High character integration — this is exactly who Artie is, a man who has sublimated all human feeling into production instinct. Quotable, thematically resonant, earns its high scores.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You want high ratings? Let's do who shot Hank Kingsley?

jokes.text: 'You didn't like Jeannie? Why didn't you say— the girl was bad news. Why didn't you say something? You could have saved me a lot of—' / 'Money?' / 'Heartache.'
jokes.setup: Artie is arguing that saying something about a friend's bad relationship choice always backfires; reveals he disliked Larry's ex-wife Jeannie
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Money?' before Larry can say 'heartache' — Artie assumes the practical concern, Larry corrects to the emotional one (then Artie notes the money concern was valid too)
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean comedic beat: Artie's 'Money?' as the anticipated completion of Larry's sentence, followed by Larry's 'Heartache' correction — then the implicit acknowledgment that money was probably also an issue — efficiently characterizes both men and their friendship. Artie sees Larry in terms of practical cost; Larry's ego requires the emotional framing. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hank, three words-- Luke and laura.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, I probably would have fired you.' / 'What do you think of Francine?' / 'I think she's great.' / [beat] 'Excuse me.' / 'I won't fire you. Tell me what you think of Francine.'
jokes.setup: Artie just admitted he would've been fired for warning Larry about Jeannie; Larry asks what Artie thinks of his current wife Francine; Artie says 'she's great' and immediately gets up to leave
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I won't fire you. Tell me what you think of Francine' — he knows Artie's evasion means Artie hates Francine too, and he's desperate to hear it while the relationship is still salvageable
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed cringe moment: Artie's instant physical retreat when asked about Francine tells us everything without a word, and Larry's 'I won't fire you' is both funny and slightly pathetic — the most power Larry can muster to compel honesty from his producer. The scene is left deliberately unresolved (Hank knocks), which is even funnier. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Now, that is what I call great television.

jokes.text: Hank's bachelor party request: 'Please, no hookers... I'm really in love. And I just don't need that kind of pressure. I mean, if the hookers are there, it's fine for the guys on crew — I don't want any part of it.'
jokes.setup: Hank is asking Larry not to arrange hookers for the bachelor party as a sign of his genuine love
jokes.punchline: His qualification — 'if the hookers are there, it's fine for the guys on crew' — reveals that his commitment isn't really a moral stance, just personal preference; he's perfectly happy to supply hookers to subordinates
jokes.explanation: A standout character comedy moment. Hank's 'no hookers' request starts as a touching declaration of love — then the qualifier 'it's fine for the guys on crew' completely reveals his class consciousness and moral flexibility. He isn't against prostitution at his bachelor party; he's against it for himself, specifically. The joke exposes so much about Hank — his self-importance, his casual treatment of crew vs. talent, his vanity disguised as virtue. Very high character integration. Quotable and rewatch-worthy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You didn't Like Jeannie? Why didn't you say-- The girl was bad news. Why didn't you Say something?

jokes.text: 'You'll rest up for tonight, right?' / 'I am going to be rested up because it's going to be wild. Nuts.' / 'We'll work our way up to wild.' / [Both] 'Nuts.'
jokes.setup: Larry is nervous about the bachelor party; Hank is enthusiastically hyping it as 'wild. Nuts.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's diplomatic 'we'll work our way up to wild' — a total retreat from Hank's enthusiasm — and then both men settling on 'nuts' as their shared, modest ambition
jokes.explanation: A quiet comedy beat about two middle-aged men negotiating what counts as a 'wild' bachelor party. 'We'll work our way up to wild' is the perfect Larry line — managing expectations, managing Hank, managing himself. The shared 'Nuts' at the end is a nice comedic button that says both men have landed at the same low bar.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I won't fire you. Tell me what you Think of Francine.

jokes.text: Strip club comedian: 'I worked at a strip club. The owner says to me, "You don't need to strip to do the comedy."' / 'We should book her on the show, Artie.' / 'As anything.' / 'As a sidekick! As a sidekick!'
jokes.setup: A female comedian is performing at the bachelor party
jokes.punchline: Her joke is mild; the real comedy is Larry and Artie immediately pivoting to talent-scouting mode at Hank's bachelor party, excitedly pitching 'sidekick!' — while Hank is presumably meant to be the center of attention
jokes.explanation: The comedian's joke itself is mild; the real comedy is meta — Larry and Artie cannot turn off their show-biz brains even at a bachelor party. They're immediately talent-scouting, escalating to 'sidekick!' — a loaded term in late-night context — while completely ignoring that this is Hank's night. Perfect industry satire.

jokes.explanation: Hank's worship of Ed McMahon — the ultimate sidekick — is a perfect character-comedy beat with meta resonance. Hank IS the Ed McMahon of his world, and his awe at the real thing is both funny and slightly sad. The line is delivered with complete sincerity which makes it land harder. The casting of actual Ed McMahon adds a layer of insider TV history comedy.

jokes.punchline: McMahon's platitude ('Never let 'em see you sweat') — a generic self-help saying he almost certainly uses regularly — and Hank's explosive endorsement ('You can take that to the bank!') which is itself a cliché, creating a comedy of mutual insincerity
jokes.explanation: McMahon delivers a platitude as wisdom; Hank receives it as revelation; and Hank's celebration uses another platitude ('You can take that to the bank') — creating a loop of hollow showbiz maxims being exchanged as genuine insight. Layered character comedy that works on multiple levels simultaneously.

jokes.explanation: A quick, economical aside that implies McMahon is already incoherent (drunk, old, or just McMahon). The total lack of concern from Larry and Artie is the comedic tone — they're not alarmed, just mildly curious. Works efficiently.

jokes.punchline: The fan thanks him as 'Mr. Brenner' — apparently thinking he's comedian David Brenner — the fan wasn't starstruck by McMahon at all, or is simply confused
jokes.explanation: A delightful misdirection — McMahon's humble 'I'm not who you think I am' turns out to be literally true; the fan thinks he's a different (lesser) celebrity entirely. It's dark for McMahon's ego and funny for the audience who gets the double meaning. Clean, economical, well-structured.

jokes.explanation: The 'saving it' excuse is a running comedy beat that works because it reveals Larry's discomfort with sincerity — he genuinely cannot bring himself to say something nice about Hank's marriage. It connects to the episode's theme. The crowd's 'toast! toast! toast!' chant escalating the pressure is a good structural choice.

jokes.explanation: The comedic structure here is the interrupted limerick — where the setup is so specific ('a feller from Dubuque') that the audience can fill in a filthy punchline themselves. The truncation is funnier than completion would be. Artie introducing this as 'off-color' and 'about fucking' with perfect gravitas is character-specific. Good economy: the joke is in what isn't said.

jokes.explanation: The Golden Horseshoe reference is an insider joke about McMahon's career trajectory — the kind of specific detail that makes comedy writing feel authentic rather than generic. McMahon's cheerful delivery of a gently damning review of the party is funny in its casualness.

jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the transparency of Larry's projection — his marriage advice is autobiographical confession. 'You'll wake up at night and not know who the fuck she is' is a great line that's simultaneously genuine wisdom and revealing self-exposure. Character integration is high because this could only be Larry.

jokes.explanation: The Porsche alternative is a well-worn observation (midlife crisis = Porsche) but the specificity of 'it won't cost you as much in the long run' redeems it — Larry has done the math, probably from personal experience. It's the kind of practical, cynical wisdom that is both funny and reveals character depth.

jokes.punchline: His defence is that he has no money — 'it's all in the restaurant' — a revelation that immediately raises more questions (what restaurant?) and suggests Hank's financial mismanagement
jokes.explanation: The restaurant detail is a perfect Hank-specific touch — it's exactly the kind of celebrity side-business vanity investment that would consume a sidekick's savings. The line is delivered as exasperation but lands as comedy because it inadvertently confirms financial recklessness. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Hey! No one gets to be happy except the great Larry Sanders. Well, let me give you a prenuptial announcement — go fuck yourself.'
jokes.setup: The bachelor party fight has escalated; Hank is furious at Larry's interference
jokes.punchline: 'Let me give you a prenuptial announcement' is a perfect wordplay construction — Hank the verbal fumbler accidentally lands a genuinely clever turn of phrase — followed by 'go fuck yourself' which is both the punchline and a character moment
jokes.explanation: The episode's most quotable line and one of its best jokes. 'Prenuptial announcement' is an inspired wordplay construction — it sounds like 'public service announcement' but filtered through wedding terminology, and it's the kind of accidental wordplay that fits perfectly with Hank's character (not usually quick-witted, but capable of stumbling onto something brilliant). The line escalates a serious emotional confrontation into comedy with one pivot. The 'go fuck yourself' payload is perfectly placed. This is 8+ territory — the wordplay is novel, structurally tight, character-specific (Hank's malapropism-adjacent verbal style), economical, and earned through a whole scene of building tension.

jokes.text: 'Keith, let's get rid of these red gels. We're not marrying two McDonald's French fries. Make it pink.'
jokes.setup: The wedding set is being prepared; the lighting is red
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'we're not marrying two McDonald's French fries' — a hilariously specific and bizarre simile for what red lighting looks like — delivered as a completely reasonable production note
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The image of 'two McDonald's French fries' is a genuinely original and specific visual metaphor for harsh red lighting — it's unexpected, vivid, and absurd in exactly the right way. The line is delivered as a completely sober production instruction, which makes it funnier. 'Make it pink' as the brisk follow-up is perfect economy. This is Artie at his best — using unexpected imagery with absolute authority. Justification for 8+: the simile is genuinely novel (French fries as a lighting note is not a standard comedy reference), the character integration is perfect (only Artie would frame this as production craft), and the economy is near-perfect. Highly quotable.

jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat — two professionals forced into proximity during a feud, with subordinates awkwardly present. Works through the discomfort of the situation rather than a specific joke construction. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Hank's bellybutton' as a legitimate lighting mark is a brilliant absurdist detail. Artie's complete seriousness about it while Larry wants to discuss a crisis is funny because it implies that in production terms, the bellybutton is a real concern. Good economy — the line is strange enough on its own.

jokes.explanation: Five words that invert a proverb and deliver an entire philosophy of Hollywood relationships. It's not the most original construction (proverb inversion is a classic comedy technique) but the delivery context and character integration make it land as genuinely Artie wisdom rather than a cheap reversal. Highly quotable and perfectly economical. The line is earned because the whole episode has been building to it.

jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Larry's complete inability to handle directness. When someone calls him out clearly, he reverts to his host persona — the chuckle is a reflex. It's a non-verbal reaction beat that says everything about his character. High character integration because only Larry, the consummate deflector, responds to an honest accusation with a talk-show host laugh.

The 'Lollipop Guild' construction is clever and specific, which saves it from being truly lazy. Scores lower on earned_vs_cheap because height jokes are an easy shortcut. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.explanation: Hank's line is the perfect combination of his character's odd dignity and the show's pop culture fabric. He wouldn't be married by the Love Boat captain — not Gavin MacLeod the man, but the character he's defined by. The line is economical and specific and funny because Hank's standard is clearly quite low (he's being married on a TV show with millions watching), yet 'Love Boat captain' is where he draws the line.

jokes.explanation: Phil gets a rare great line — 'but can you trust them?' about a television audience is both absurd and philosophically interesting (TV witnesses are passive, anonymous). The construction is tight: setup establishes the absurd premise, punchline flips it with an even more absurd paranoid concern. Good economy and originality.

jokes.explanation: The casting of Alex Trebek as officiant is a great industry-insider joke. The show consistently uses celebrity as social currency, and here that logic is extended to legal/sacred ceremony — Trebek's Jeopardy! credibility is treated as wedding-officiant credibility. The audience reaction (loud applause) within the show is also funny.

jokes.explanation: An excellent celebrity-specific joke: Trebek cannot help but be Trebek, framing the wedding as a Jeopardy! answer. It's perfectly integrated with the real celebrity's persona — you couldn't say this about any other officiant — and the comedy is in the total inappropriateness of game-show format applied to a solemn ceremony. The line 'today, the answer is' before revealing bride and groom is genuinely clever structure. High character integration (could ONLY be Trebek), high originality, well-earned. This is 8+ territory.

jokes.punchline: Trebek frames the couple as a Jeopardy! 'answer' — using the show's signature reversed question-answer format for a wedding ceremony. It's the joke of casting Trebek, fully committed.
jokes.explanation: The Jeopardy! framing ('today the answer is...') applied to wedding introductions is a clean, well-executed joke that rewards the casting choice. It works as a standalone joke and as the payoff to the Alex Trebek choice. The ceremony-game-show fusion is absurdist but internally consistent.

jokes.text: Hank breaks down reading his vows, can't continue, then pulls out notecards: '[laughter as he reads] "Margaret..." / [Laughter] / "I thought I knew sunshine, but I knew only shade."'
jokes.setup: Hank begins his vows emotionally; breaks down completely; the audience laughs at his breakdown; he then produces a notecard with the vows written out
jokes.punchline: The vows themselves are revealed to be written-out notecards — beautiful, formal, and slightly absurd poetry that Hank reads stiffly — which gets laughter from the in-show audience
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in cringe-comedy structure. The joke accumulates in layers: Hank's sincere emotional breakdown → scattered laughter from the audience (uncomfortable) → the notecard reveal (he prepared but fell apart) → the formal, slightly purple prose he reads ('I knew only shade') getting laughter from the audience even though it's beautiful. The comedy and the pathos are inseparable here — Tambor makes you feel both simultaneously. The in-show audience laughing at Hank's genuine emotion is meta-cruel, and the show is aware of it. Very high character integration — this is quintessential Hank: simultaneously over-prepared and emotionally overwhelmed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry

jokes.text: 'If you like this wedding, maybe we can have ours on the show.' / [beat] / 'I'm... joking.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine are watching Hank's wedding reception and finding it moving
jokes.punchline: Larry suggests they get married on the show — then immediately has to clarify 'I'm joking' — the pause before the clarification is the joke: he may not be joking, or Francine's reaction required retreat
jokes.explanation: The episode's most emotionally resonant joke. The suggestion — getting married on the show — is pure Larry Sanders: incapable of separating his personal life from the professional spectacle. The 'I'm joking' retreat is funnier than the suggestion, because the beat before it implies either genuine desire or Francine's horrified reaction (or both). It also crystallizes the Larry/Francine relationship: she has to live with a man who might, non-jokingly, want to televise their wedding. Very high character integration. The awkward silence IS the joke here.

The Don Johnson/Melanie Griffith reference is period-specific and moderately funny as a non-sequitur response to a romantic suggestion. Not especially crafted but serves the scene.

The 'I've asked you nicely' implies this is a recurring problem, which makes it funnier. The comedy works because it lets emotion breathe before puncturing it — perfect structure for the show's tone.

The gap between the vows' purple poetry and how people relate to them (as entertainment, not romance) is the joke.

jokes.text: Hank demands Larry re-read the vows at the reception: 'I'd like you to read them again. Just one more time.' / Larry (incredulous): 'Are you serious?' / They read: 'But I only knew like.' / Margaret: 'Oh, beautiful.'
jokes.setup: The wedding is over. Hank wants to relive his finest moment.
jokes.punchline: Hank makes Larry re-read the wedding vows at the reception as a performance piece. The gathering crowd treating this as an encore is both sweet and completely bizarre.
jokes.explanation: A good callback beat — the vows that were embarrassing during the ceremony become, by the reception, the highlight Hank wants to replay. 'But I only knew like' as an encore-worthy line captures Hank's complete comfort with his own sentimentality.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry for questioning why she was marrying you. It's so clear that she's marrying you because of the man you are.'
jokes.setup: Larry is apologizing to Hank for his bachelor party intervention
jokes.punchline: The apology sounds sincere but 'because of the man you are' is subtly ambiguous — in Larry's mouth, this compliment is a maze, and the audience isn't sure if Larry means it or is still being condescending
jokes.explanation: A mild irony beat — the ambiguity of Larry's sincerity is the joke, but it's subtle enough that it may not register as comedy for all viewers. Works as character texture more than a clear punchline.

jokes.text: 'Meet my dad, Harold Dolan.' / 'Hey, there, the pleasure is all yours!' / [Laughing] 'Just kidding.'
jokes.setup: Margaret's father — who was absent for the entire ceremony — is introduced at the reception
jokes.punchline: Harold's first words are 'The pleasure is all yours!' — the wrong way round from 'the pleasure is all mine' — then 'Just kidding,' implying he knows exactly what he said; plus his late arrival compounds the joke
jokes.explanation: A perfect final joke for the episode. Harold's 'the pleasure is all yours!' is an inspired inversion of the polite formula — it's simultaneously rude (placing the pleasure obligation on others) and then defused with 'just kidding,' but the 'just kidding' makes it worse because it confirms he knew exactly what he was doing. The episode ends on a gag that introduces a character who is immediately, irredeemably Hank-adjacent in his social obliviousness. Artie's 'Jesus Christ' is the perfect button. The late arrival + the wrong-way greeting + the casual 'just kidding' = a beautifully constructed closing beat.

tmdb_overview: Larry tries to decide about warning an elated Hank about his new bride when the ""Hey now!"" guy announces he's going to marry a younger woman he has just recently met.
